parts.partTitle: Stack vs. Heap: Where Your Data Resides

beats.headline: Declaring a primitive stores raw bits. Declaring an object stores an address.
beats.subline: Understanding Stack vs Heap dictates how fast your Java application runs.
beats.narration: Assigning int score equals 100 reserves raw binary bits directly in memory. Assigning a user object creates a pointer address pointing to the heap. Here is how stack and heap dictate Java execution speed.

beats.title: Stack vs. Heap Memory Layout
beats.subtitle: Local variables sit on thread stack frames; objects reside on the shared heap

nodes.label: Thread Stack
nodes.detail: Holds local primitive values & object memory addresses directly

nodes.label: Address Reference
nodes.detail: 64-bit pointer linking stack variable to heap location

nodes.label: Shared JVM Heap
nodes.detail: Stores actual object payload, fields & string pool instances

nodes.label: Garbage Collector
nodes.detail: Reclaims heap memory when zero references point to an object

beats.narration: Every thread gets a stack storing method frames and local variables. Local primitives sit directly in stack slots, while object reference variables hold memory addresses pointing to objects dynamic allocated on the shared heap.

beats.title: Field Defaults vs. Uninitialized Local Variables

top.label: Class Fields (Heap)
points: Fields on heap get automatic default values
Primitives get 0 or false, references get null

bottom.label: Local Variables (Stack)
points: Stack slots contain leftover stack garbage
Compiler rejects reads before explicit assignment

beats.narration: Class fields residing on the heap get automatic zero initialization. But local variables on the stack get no default values at all. Reading an uninitialized local variable fails at compile time immediately.

beats.title: Inspecting Primitive vs Reference Locations

steps.explanation: Field id is a primitive, but because it belongs to MemoryDemo, it resides on the heap inside the object.
Local double balance sits directly inside the method stack frame as pure binary bits.
Local user reference sits on stack, but its string character content resides in the heap pool.

beats.narration: Look at the memory location rules. Local primitive balance sits directly inside the method stack frame. But field id resides inside object storage on the heap, even though id is a primitive.

beats.title: Memory Layout Mastered
takeaways: Primitives store values directly; references store heap addresses
Local variables sit on stack frames; heap holds all objects
Class fields auto-initialize to zero; local variables do not

beats.headline: Calculating 0.1 plus 0.2 in Java yields 0.30000000000000004.
beats.subline: Binary IEEE 754 precision will corrupt floating point financial software.
beats.narration: Evaluating zero point one plus zero point two using double in Java produces zero point three zero zero zero four. Here is why binary floating point breaks monetary calculations.

beats.title: Silent Wrap Around vs Safe Math

steps.explanation: Java arithmetic never throws on numeric overflow! High bits drop and values wrap to negative minimum.
Throws ArithmeticException instantly when arithmetic exceeds boundaries.

beats.narration: Adding one to maximum int wrap around silently to negative two billion with zero warning. For financial counters or critical arithmetic, use Math dot addExact to trigger exceptions on overflow.

beats.title: Floating Point vs exact Financial Math

top.label: double / float
points: Fractions repeat infinitely in base-2 binary
Rounding errors accumulate across billing cycles

bottom.label: BigDecimal / Cents
points: BigDecimal initialized from String preserves exact digits
Or store monetary values as primitive long cents

beats.narration: Base two floating point cannot represent decimal fractions like zero point one exactly. For financial calculations, build BigDecimal from string literals or store monetary amounts as long integer cents.

beats.title: Running Numeric Tests
beats.caption: Demonstrating overflow wrap and exact overflow exceptions

lines.text: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: integer overflow

beats.narration: Standard integer addition wraps around silently into negative numbers. Calling Math dot addExact aborts execution immediately with an exception, stopping corrupted data from hitting database tables.

beats.title: Primitives Guarded
takeaways: Integer arithmetic wraps silently using two's complement
Use Math.addExact() to prevent silent numeric corruption
Never use float or double for money; use BigDecimal or cents

beats.narration: Those are primitive numeric limits. In Part 3, we dive into autoboxing traps, silent null pointer crashes, and the JVM integer cache.

beats.headline: Integer a equals 100 returns true, but Integer x equals 200 returns false.
beats.subline: Comparing wrapper objects with double equals creates subtle production bugs.
beats.narration: Comparing two Integer object variables assigned to 100 returns true using double equals. But assigning both to 200 returns false. This bug stems from the JVM Integer cache.

beats.title: The Integer Cache & Null Pointer Traps

steps.explanation: Integer.valueOf caches values from -128 through 127. Both variables share the exact same pooled reference.
Values outside cache range allocate distinct heap objects. Always use .equals() for wrapper identity.
Implicit unboxing calls count.intValue() on null, causing an instant NullPointerException.

beats.narration: The JVM caches Integer objects between minus 128 and 127. Outside that range, double equals checks reference memory addresses. Furthermore, unboxing a null wrapper invokes intValue on null, throwing a NullPointerException.

beats.title: Loop Performance: Primitive vs. Boxed Wrapper

top.label: Boxed Wrapper Loop
points: Allocates millions of temporary Long instances

bottom.label: Primitive Loop
points: Zero heap allocation and zero GC overhead

beats.narration: Declaring sum as wrapper Long inside a loop repeatedly unboxes and re-boxes numbers. That allocates millions of short lived heap objects. Using primitive long keeps calculations inside CPU registers.

beats.title: JMH Benchmark Results
beats.caption: Comparing execution runtime between Long and long

lines.text: Benchmark               Mode  Cnt   Score   Error  Units
# Primitive execution runs 13x faster with 0 GC overhead!

beats.narration: Microbenchmarks confirm that primitive arithmetic runs over ten times faster than boxed wrapper iterations. Avoid object wrapper types inside heavy calculation loops.

beats.title: Wrappers Demystified
takeaways: Always use .equals() for wrappers due to -128 to 127 caching
Unboxing null wrapper objects throws NullPointerException
Use primitives in loops to prevent heap allocation churn

parts.partTitle: String Pool, Type Casting & Modern var

beats.headline: Comparing string input using double equals can bypass authentication logic.
beats.subline: String literals reuse the constant pool; dynamically constructed strings do not.
beats.narration: Comparing string variables with double equals breaks when text comes from JSON payloads or file inputs. Here is how the String Constant Pool dictates reference equality.

beats.title: String Constant Pool Architecture
beats.subtitle: Literals share pooled references; explicit constructor calls bypass pooling

nodes.label: Literal 'a'
nodes.detail: String a = "Java" points to constant pool

nodes.label: Literal 'b'
nodes.detail: String b = "Java" reuses existing pool entry

nodes.label: String Constant Pool
nodes.detail: Special heap segment storing unique immutable string values

nodes.label: Explicit 'new String()'
nodes.detail: Forces new heap allocation outside string pool

beats.narration: String literals point directly to shared string objects inside the pool on the heap. But dynamic strings or explicit constructor calls create separate heap objects, causing reference comparisons to return false.

beats.title: Casting Rules & Modern var Type Inference

steps.explanation: Explicit cast (int) truncates fractional digits towards zero without rounding.
Infers type at compile time from right hand initializer. Remains 100% statically typed!
var requires an explicit non-null initializer and cannot be used for fields or parameters.

beats.narration: Narrowing numeric types requires an explicit cast that truncates fractional decimals toward zero. Meanwhile, Java 10 introduced var to infer local variable types from initializers while remaining 100 percent statically typed.

beats.title: Disassembling var Bytecode
beats.caption: Proving var emits identical bytecode to explicit types

lines.text: 2: astore_1      // Stores reference into local variable 1
Identical bytecode generated as explicit String declaration!

beats.narration: Disassembling compiled code with javap proves that var generates identical bytecode compared to explicit type declarations. It is compile time syntactic sugar with zero runtime performance impact.

beats.title: Chapter Complete! Run the Lab
takeaways: Always use .equals() for strings to compare text instead of pool pointers
Narrowing numerical casts truncate fractional decimals without rounding
var provides static type inference for local variables at compile time
